text: ABSTRACT India’s Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework produces a large collection of company disclosures containing text and numerical information. Reviewing this collection manually requires analysts to locate relevant statements, identify supporting figures and compare reporting across companies. Existing language tools can recognise topics, retrieve answers or detect persuasive wording, but disclosure review also needs a clear connection to filed evidence. GRASP provides a connected workflow for this purpose. Public filings are collected and stored with company identity, reporting period and context. Narrative text segments receive filing- derived principle labels and support a domain-adapted BERT classifier. Word lists and MPNet sentence similarity identify potentially vague language, while numerical and assurance rules create linked review records. A fixed Transparency Score combines Completeness, Specificity, Clarity and mapped Sustainable Development Goal coverage, and the service layer presents company and sector comparisons. The labelled corpus contains 42,409 text segments. On 6,201 test text segments from 175 companies excluded from supervised training, the recovered classifier reaches 93.00% Top-1 agreement and macro-F1 of 0.9158 against the taxonomy-derived labels. The Transparency Score has a Pearson correlation of 0.6314 with historical ratings for 20 companies. Application results cover 1,164 company scores and demonstrate review at company, financial- sector and wider sector levels. The outcome is an inspectable disclosure-analysis workflow that brings source records, principle assignments and visible score calculations together for consistent review. Keywords: BRSR; disclosure analysis; weak supervision; BERT; vagueness detection; Transparency Score.

text: CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION 1.1 Introduction Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) gives Indian listed companies a common structure for reporting environmental, social and governance information. A filing contains descriptive answers as well as numerical items about subjects such as energy, emissions, water, employment and business conduct. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced the reporting requirement through its 2021 circular [1]. The reporting structure creates an opportunity to study disclosure quality across companies using a common set of questions. A common reporting format does not make a large collection easy to review. A data analyst still needs to locate relevant text, identify the reporting principle, check supporting figures and compare the result with suitable companies. Manual review becomes difficult when hundreds of reports contain similar wording, repeated answers and different reporting periods. A clear statement can also describe an intention without providing evidence of progress. GRASP, the Greenwashing Recognition and Scoring Pipeline, connects filing collection, text analysis, numerical review and company comparison. The application organises public filing data and produces records that a reviewer can inspect. The system assigns BRSR principles to text segments, flags potentially vague language, links selected claims with filed figures and calculates a Transparency Score with a visible component breakdown. Three terms have fixed meanings in this report. A report or filing is one company submission for a reporting year. A fact is one stored reporting item together with its concept, value and context. A text segment is the narrative content extracted from a fact and used for language analysis. Dataset counts refer to text segments unless a table explicitly states companies, filings or grouped examples. These units are kept separate because one filing can supply many facts and text segments. 1.2 Motivation The practical need is to make supporting evidence easier to find. Consider a company statement that emissions have reduced. A phrase detector may recognise a reduction claim, but a reviewer also needs the relevant emissions value, comparison period and unit. Showing the sentence beside the reported numbers creates a more useful review record than a language label alone.

text: A second motivation is consistency. Analysts may interpret the same disclosure differently when the principle assignment and score calculation are not visible. Filing-derived labels provide a repeatable starting point for model training. Recording the label source makes it possible to assess whether the classifier behaves differently on explicitly tagged answers and concept-mapped answers. The third motivation is comparison at scale. A company score is easier to interpret when the calculation and peer group are available. A financial company and a manufacturer can have different reporting patterns. Sector comparisons therefore accompany the score, while the original component values remain available for review. The intended use is evidence-supported disclosure screening rather than an automatic finding of misconduct. 1.3 Problem Definition The problem is to turn a large collection of public BRSR filings into a consistent and inspectable disclosure-review workflow. The workflow must preserve filing context, classify narrative content under nine principles, identify language requiring closer review, expose relevant numerical evidence and summarise company disclosures using a reproducible score. The input is a structured BRSR filing containing company identity, reporting dates, narrative answers and numerical facts. The outputs are stored filing records, principle probabilities, vagueness and filing-consistency review records, four Transparency Score components and company or sector comparisons. The core engineering requirement is traceability: a reported output should be linked to its source filing and calculation. Success is assessed using separate evidence for separate functions. Principle classification is compared with taxonomy-derived labels on companies excluded from supervised training. The text-vagueness detector is compared with the available development and AI annotation sets. The score is compared with the historical human-rating cohort. Application records demonstrate coverage and examples of operation; those records are not model-accuracy measurements. 1.4 Existing Systems Existing approaches include keyword dictionaries, supervised text classifiers, sentence-embedding methods and large language model assistants. Dictionaries can identify phrases such as commitments or targets, but a word match alone provides little information about the quality of

text: supporting evidence. Sentence embeddings compare meaning and can group related disclosures without requiring a labelled training set. Domain-specific transformer models, including ClimateBERT, improve the representation of climate-related language through additional pretraining [2]. Retrieval and language model systems such as ChatReport and ESGReveal support question answering and information extraction from sustainability reports [3], [4]. These methods are useful building blocks, but the task addressed in this report also requires filing context, numerical records and transparent company-level aggregation. Manual spreadsheets and dashboards can compare disclosed values after extraction. The main difficulty is the effort required to connect extracted values with narrative claims and to keep the same calculation across a national collection. GRASP combines these functions in one data and service architecture. 1.5 Lacunae in Existing Systems The first gap concerns the link between a statement and supporting evidence. Identifying an environmental topic does not establish whether a numerical item supports the statement. A useful screening system should keep the sentence, figure and filing context available for inspection. The second gap concerns the source of training labels. A reported classification score is difficult to interpret if the label creation process is unclear. BRSR offers explicit principle tags and question concepts, but these sources differ. The dataset therefore records whether a label came from a PrincipleAxis tag, a concept map or a principle-specific note. The third gap concerns the meaning of an aggregate score. A single value can hide whether the result comes from broad reporting coverage, specific evidence or clear language. GRASP displays the four component values and provides comparisons within recorded sector groups. This design connects the score with the underlying reporting behaviour. 1.6 Relevance of the Project For an analyst, the workflow brings text, figures and review signals into one interface. For a researcher, the saved dataset and evaluation artifacts make the label source and test population explicit. For a company preparing a report, the component breakdown can identify which parts of

text: CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE SURVEY 2.1 Brief Overview Research on sustainability disclosure analysis spans language representation, topic classification, evidence retrieval, greenwashing screening and company-level reporting. The review focuses on how each approach supplies a useful part of the GRASP workflow. A model that recognises climate-related language solves a different task from a system that retrieves an answer or calculates a company score. Published results are therefore interpreted in the context of the original task and dataset. The selected literature includes foundational transformer methods, climate-specific language models, weak supervision, disclosure assistants and an Indian BRSR study. This combination explains both the language-processing choices and the need for a filing-centred application. Table 2.1 summarises the main technical connections. 2.2 Related Works and Research Papers Referred 2.2.1 General language models and domain adaptation BERT uses bidirectional transformer representations learned through pretraining and then adapts those representations to a supervised task [7]. In a classification setting, a task-specific head converts the encoded text into class scores. This architecture supports the nine-principle classifier because one text segment can be represented and assigned a probability for each principle. Gururangan et al. studied continued pretraining on domain and task text [8]. The central idea is that general pretraining can be followed by adaptation to the vocabulary and writing style of a specific corpus. GRASP follows that model-development pattern before principle fine-tuning. The available experiments do not isolate a causal percentage-point gain from adaptation alone. A controlled plain-BERT versus adapted-BERT experiment would require otherwise identical data and training settings. MPNet combines masked and permuted pretraining objectives [19]. Sentence-transformer models provide sentence-level vectors that can be compared using cosine similarity [9]. In GRASP, MPNet supplies semantic comparisons for vagueness analysis and a zero-shot principle

text: comparator. The supervised BERT classifier and zero-shot comparator use different learning conditions and are described accordingly. 2.2.2 Climate-related language and greenwashing analysis ClimateBERT applies additional pretraining to climate-related text [2]. ClimaText provides a dataset for identifying climate-change topics [12]. These contributions demonstrate the value of specialist language data, while also showing that topic recognition and evidence verification remain separate questions. A sentence can clearly concern climate change without proving that a stated action has occurred. Bingler et al. investigated the characteristics of corporate climate disclosures, including general language and selective disclosure [13], [14]. The later study connects disclosure language with climate initiatives, emissions and reputation-related information. This line of research motivates the distinction between a statement that sounds convincing and a statement supported by concrete evidence. ClimateBERT-NetZero focuses on identifying and assessing net-zero and reduction targets [15]. Vinella et al. study language models for greenwashing detection [16]. These tasks contribute ideas about commitments, specificity and classification, but no published metric is transferred into the GRASP results table. Each model has a different evaluation population and label definition. The survey by Calamai et al. brings together text-based greenwashing methods and helps distinguish linguistic signals from stronger evidence about company conduct [5]. The GRASP detector is therefore presented as a set of review signals. The audited numerical results concern its text-vagueness subdetector, rather than an independently validated determination of greenwashing across all signals. 2.2.3 Disclosure assistants and information extraction ChatReport uses large language model tools to support sustainability disclosure analysis [3]. ESGReveal extracts structured information from ESG reports [4]. These systems show how language models can reduce the effort of finding and organising relevant information. GRASP instead begins with structured filing facts and keeps the relationship between narrative text and numerical items in a relational database.

text: The distinction is practical. Answer generation is useful for a question asked by a reviewer, while a structured pipeline can repeatedly apply the same calculation to a complete filing collection. GRASP retains a supervised classifier for principle assignment and explicit rules for inspectable review records. This choice makes the source and calculation visible without requiring generated explanations for every stored item. 2.2.4 Indian reporting, weak labels and evaluation The Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad study analyses BRSR disclosures submitted by 1,012 Indian businesses [6]. It provides relevant national reporting context and demonstrates the value of studying disclosure patterns across a large collection. Shankar and Xu examine automated greenwashing detection in Indian corporate sustainability reports [17]. These studies place the application in the Indian reporting setting. Snorkel describes the use of programmatic weak supervision to create training labels [10]. GRASP does not implement a Snorkel generative label model; the relevant idea is the explicit treatment of automatically derived labels as weak supervision. PrincipleAxis tags, concept maps and principle- specific notes supply three recorded label sources. Kapoor and Narayanan explain how leakage can distort scientific machine-learning evaluation [11]. GRASP therefore separates companies during supervised training and reports source-wise and concept-exclusion diagnostics. Repeated text across different companies and earlier encoder adaptation are separate considerations from supervised company overlap. Recording these distinctions makes the reported result easier to interpret. Table 2. 1. text: CHAPTER 8: CONCLUSION GRASP connects public BRSR filings with a structured disclosure-review workflow. The implementation preserves company, period and context information, builds filing-derived principle labels, applies a recovered BERT classifier, generates language and filing-consistency review records, and calculates a Transparency Score with four visible components. The service layer makes these outputs available for company inspection and peer comparison. The approved company-disjoint evaluation contains 6,201 text segments from 175 companies. The classifier reaches 93.00% Top-1 agreement and macro-F1 0.9158 against taxonomy-derived labels. Source-wise evaluation shows 63.35% on Section B, 95.15% on Section C and 90.72% on principle-specific notes. These distinctions are central to the interpretation of the overall result. The fixed vagueness detector reaches F1 0.7436 on the development set and 0.6885 in the AI-label comparison. The Transparency Score has Pearson correlation 0.6314 with the historical 20- company human-rating cohort. Application results connect these model evaluations with use at four levels: one worked company, selected financial companies, the complete financial-sector group and all recorded sectors. The saved score collection covers 1,164 companies. The component breakdown shows how coverage, evidence markers, language flags and mapped goal breadth contribute to each result. This combination provides a practical basis for consistent disclosure screening and evidence review. 8.1 Limitations Training labels are taxonomy-derived weak labels, including AI-assisted concept assignments. High agreement on recurring Section C content does not by itself establish broad semantic understanding. The concept-exclusion results and lower Section B agreement make this distinction visible. Company separation is verified for supervised fine-tuning; the legacy adaptation corpus has a separate exposure concern. The measured detector results concern text vagueness, and the newer annotation set is AI- generated. The human-score comparison is small and comes from one historical source with unrecorded blinding. The score uses a fixed database concept universe and a fixed principle-to- SDG map. Sector assignment, mixed-year snapshots and the limited paired-year subset should be considered when interpreting application comparisons.

text: Current application screens and approved research snapshots can differ as code or data changes. Publication tables remain tied to the saved audit artifacts. Broader deployment requires controlled upload, security, concurrency, accessibility and response-time testing. 8.2 Future Scope This work can be extended using multiple levels. At the data level, ingestion can include unstructured annexures and charts while retaining source locations and reporting context. At the model level, a train-company-only adaptation corpus and controlled plain-BERT comparison can isolate representation effects. Larger concept-disjoint evaluations and independently annotated cross-cutting text can improve understanding of generalisation. At the validation level, new blinded annotations can be collected for the complete review workflow and for company scores, with reference instructions and agreement documented before evaluation. Score calibration should use separate data from the final evaluation. At the operational level, timed analyst tasks, accessibility checks, load tests and measured computing energy can support stronger deployment and sustainability claims. At the longitudinal level, additional annual cycles can extend the eight-company paired analysis into a wider panel with consistent reporting definitions. At the policy level, the filing-centred approach can be studied under other structured sustainability standards, including international frameworks. Such extensions should preserve the distinction between disclosure quality, model support and independently verified company performance.
